edges.effect_quant: The best current pooled evidence suggests that heavier screen exposure is associated with higher odds of developing myopia, with risk increasing as daily digital-device time rises. Newer dose-response meta-analyses show higher myopia odds with each additional hour of screen time and stronger risk at higher-exposure categories.
edges.population: children and adolescents with higher daily digital screen exposure
edges.mechanism: Prolonged screen use combines near work, shorter viewing distance, lower blink rate, and often reduced outdoor time, all of which plausibly push refractive development toward incident myopia.
edges.summary: This is a credible modifiable-risk edge. Screen time is probably not the sole driver of childhood myopia, but the better pooled evidence now supports it as a harmful contributor to incident myopia risk.
edges.caveats: Most of the evidence is observational and entangled with education, indoor lifestyle, and less time outdoors. The edge is best read as a risk signal rather than proof that screens alone cause the myopia epidemic.

evidence.citation: Lee YJ et al 2025 JAMA Netw Open
evidence.notes: Digital Screen Time and Myopia: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis.
